Suede is a type of soft, velvety leather with a fuzzy surface. It is used to make shoes, jackets, bags, and many other products.
What suede actually is

An animal's skin has two sides: the outer side (the part that faced the world, exposed to sun and air) and the inner side (the part that was touching the animal's body). Regular leather — the kind used in belts, hard-soled shoes, and briefcases — uses that tough outer surface. Suede is different. It is made from the inner side of the skin.

That inner surface is then sanded or buffed, which causes tiny fibers to stand up from the surface. These upright fibers are called the nap. The nap is what gives suede its soft, fuzzy, velvety feel — almost like a dry velvet fabric.
Which animals does it come from?

Suede can come from lamb, calf (young cow), deer, pig, or goat. Lamb suede is the most common and highly regarded — it is exceptionally soft and fine. In general, the younger the animal, the softer and more delicate the suede tends to be.
What it looks and feels like

Suede has a consistently soft, slightly fuzzy surface. It is not shiny like polished leather — it has a matte, almost dusty look. The color appears rich and deep.

Here is a distinctive feature: if you run your finger across suede in one direction, the nap flattens and the surface looks slightly lighter in color. Run your finger back the other way, and the fibers stand back up, making the color look richer and darker. This directional behavior of the nap is one of suede's most recognizable characteristics.
How suede differs from regular leather

—Regular leather (full-grain)Suede

Regular leather uses the outer side of the skin. That outer layer is dense, tough, naturally smooth, and quite resistant to water and scratches. It's the stronger of the two.

Suede, using the inner side, is:

  • Significantly softer and more flexible
  • Lighter in weight
  • Velvety in texture rather than smooth
  • More delicate and easier to damage
  • Much more vulnerable to water and stains

Think of it this way: regular leather is like a hard shell; suede is the soft lining inside.
Suede vs. Nubuck — an important distinction

This confuses a lot of people. Nubuck also has a soft, fuzzy nap — but it is buffed from the outer side of the hide (usually calfskin). Because the outer side is naturally tougher and more tightly structured, nubuck is slightly more durable and firmer than suede, even though both feel soft and look similar at first glance.

Simple rule to remember: Suede = inner side of skin = softer and more delicate. Nubuck = outer side of skin = slightly tougher and more resistant.
What suede is used for

Suede is prized in fashion and design because of its luxurious feel and elegant, understated appearance. Common uses include:

  • Footwear — Suede shoes and boots are extremely popular. The classic desert boot, Chelsea boots, and many casual sneakers are made in suede.
  • Clothing — Suede jackets, coats, skirts, and trousers appear frequently in fashion. A suede jacket has a distinctive soft drape and warmth.
  • Bags and accessories — Purses, wallets, and gloves made from suede have a premium, soft-to-the-touch feel.
  • Furniture upholstery — Sofas and chairs are sometimes upholstered in suede for a rich, comfortable appearance.
  • Linings and interiors — Because of its softness, suede is often used to line the insides of jewelry boxes, instrument cases, and high-end bags.
Suede's biggest weakness: it's delicate

The inner side of skin is not built to face the world — and that shows. Suede has real vulnerabilities you need to know about.

Water is suede's enemy. Even a light rain can leave visible water marks on suede. Oil and liquid stains are very hard to remove and can permanently discolor the surface. This is why suede products often come with a recommendation to spray them with a waterproofing spray before first use — this creates a protective barrier on the fibers.

Dirt and scuffs are also a problem. The nap traps dust and can flatten in areas that get rubbed often (like the toe of a shoe or the bottom of a bag).

Suede is maintained with a special suede brush — a brush with stiff bristles used to lift the flattened nap back up and to remove dry surface dirt. You should never scrub suede with a wet cloth the way you would clean regular leather or fabric.

For this reason, suede products are generally considered "dry weather" items. Many people avoid wearing suede shoes on rainy days entirely.
Faux suede (synthetic suede)

Because real suede is expensive and requires careful care, many products today use faux suede — also called synthetic suede, microsuede, or vegan suede. This is an artificial material made from very fine polyester or nylon microfibers woven together to mimic the look and feel of real suede. Well-known versions include brands called Ultrasuede and Alcantara (used in luxury car interiors).

Faux suede is:

  • More affordable than real suede
  • Easier to clean
  • More resistant to water and stains
  • Slightly less soft than the finest real suede
  • More uniform in appearance (real suede has natural variation in texture and color)

It is widely used in furniture, car interiors, clothing, and fashion accessories. When a product says "suede" at a low price point, it is often faux suede.
How to tell real suede from faux suede

Real suede has a natural, slightly irregular texture — the fibers are not perfectly uniform. It also breathes (allows air through) and has the natural variation that comes from an animal hide. Faux suede tends to look slightly more uniform and synthetic under close inspection, and it does not breathe as naturally.
The word used in everyday speech

When people say something is "suede" or "in suede," they simply mean it has that soft, velvety, napped surface — whether from real leather or synthetic material. "A pair of suede boots" immediately tells you those boots are soft, matte-textured, and require gentle care. It signals a certain luxurious softness and a slightly fashion-forward or classic aesthetic.
Summary

Suede is leather made from the inner side of animal skin, sanded to produce a soft, fuzzy, velvety surface called the nap. It is softer and more flexible than regular leather, but also more delicate — it marks easily, absorbs water, and needs careful maintenance. It is used in shoes, clothing, bags, and furniture. Synthetic versions (faux suede) replicate its appearance at lower cost and with greater durability. The word "suede" signals softness, a matte velvety texture, and a certain refined quality in any product it describes.
